Aleksandar Vucic, leader of the right-wing Serbian Progressive Party, waits to vote in Belgrade on October 25, 2026 [Petr David Josek/AP Photo]By Armin AljovicPublished On 26 Oct 202626 Oct 2026
Aleksandar Vucic, who has shaped Serbia’s political life for more than a decade, has lost snap parliamentary elections to a student-led movement that led protests against him for almost two years.
After a heated race, Vucic conceded defeat to the Student List in Sunday’s elections, which saw voter turnout reach its highest level in more than 30 years.
Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4From the streets to the ballot box: Serbia’s students hope for election winlist 2 of 4Thousands gather at final student-led rally ahead of Serbia electionlist 3 of 4Serbia’s snap election: Can student-led protests end Vucic’s grip on power?list 4 of 4Serbia votes in election pitting longtime leader against student movementend of list
“It is clear that we have lost these elections,” the leader of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) told supporters after a sample of votes showed his electoral list was expected to win 105 seats in Serbia’s 250-member parliament, compared with 135 to 140 for the Student List.
The student movement emerged after 16 people were killed when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad on November 1, 2024.
The youth-led protests grew into a broader wave of social unrest and evolved into the Student List political platform, which promised to tackle corruption, depoliticise public institutions and restore citizens’ rights.
During the election campaign, the movement was led by Ilija Srdanovic, a professor at the Faculty of Medicine in Novi Sad.

Magistrate Muhammed Krubally follows proceedings on his computer in the courtroom [Kaddy Jawo/Al Jazeera]By Kaddy JawoPublished On 26 Oct 202626 Oct 2026
Banjul, the Gambia – It is still early when Magistrate Muhammed Krubally arrives at the Banjul Magistrates’ Court.
Before the first case, his clerk goes over the day’s proceedings, running through the files and making sure everything is in place. Krubally listens, asks questions, and prepares to preside.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Gambian leader pledges halt to rolling blackouts as protests turn violentlist 2 of 3Former ‘death squad’ leader appears in military trial in The Gambialist 3 of 3The Gambia to pay reparations to ex-dictator’s victims from sale of US mansionend of list
Then he enters a packed courtroom, where lawyers, witnesses and relatives have gathered for a criminal case.
The room falls quiet.
Krubally cannot see the people before him, but he can hear them. A lawyer rises. A witness speaks. Papers move across the room. His clerk is nearby.
At his desk, his computer speaks back to him.
Krubally uses JAWS, or Job Access With Speech, a screen reader that allows him to navigate his computer and read documents and judgements.
“This makes my job very easy,” he tells Al Jazeera.
He also uses AI-enabled smart glasses to access information and carry out tasks independently.
But technology is only part of how he works.
He listens for voices, remembers details and follows the rhythm of proceedings, building a picture of the courtroom through sound. When necessary, he relies on his clerk.
At 41, Krubally says he has presided over more than 1,000 civil and criminal cases since joining the bench.
In 2016, he became the Gambia’s first visually impaired magistrate. The...

Israelis will head to the polls on Tuesday for legislative elections.
The vote, the first since the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023 and the subsequent genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, is being called one of the most important in its history.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3US support for Israel continues three years into the genocide in Gazalist 2 of 3Israel’s deadline to close UK consulate in East Jerusalem nearslist 3 of 3Protesters in Colombia rally against ties with Israelend of list
It will determine the direction of Israel’s government as the country remains embroiled in multiple years-long conflicts, faces growing international criticism and grapples with deepening polarisation at home.
Here are five things to know about the upcoming election:
Which are the main parties and what do opinion polls suggest?
Any party clearing an electoral threshold of 3.25 percent enters parliament, whose term lasts four years.
There are two main blocs vying to lead the next government.
The first is the pro-Netanyahu coalition, led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and joined by several far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties. These include United Torah Judaism (UTJ) and Shas – both conservative religious parties – and Otzma Yehudi and Religious Zionism-Zehut, led respectively by far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.

Election workers process mail-in ballots at the Registrar of Voters facility in San Diego, California, US, on October 23, 2026 [Mike Blake/Reuters]By Al Jazeera Staff and ReutersPublished On 26 Oct 202626 Oct 2026
A United States appeals court has expressed doubt over the Department of Justice’s lawsuit against California, which seeks to force the state to throw out mail-in ballots it has deemed likely to go to noncitizens.
Circuit Judge Mark Bennett said on Sunday the three-judge panel would issue a decision as soon as possible, following a rare weekend oral argument.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Trump administration sues California over noncitizens on voter rollslist 2 of 3US judge blocks federal operations seeking to identify non-citizen voterslist 3 of 3Will ICE agents play a role in the 2026 US midterm elections?end of list
But Bennett, an appointee of Republican President Donald Trump, voiced concern that the lawsuit would not hold up to scrutiny.
He pointed to the Elections Clause in the US Constitution, which allows states — not the federal government — to administer elections.
“It seems to me that you want us to issue an injunction that is entirely inconsistent with the law that the California legislature has adopted pursuant to the Elections Clause,” Bennett told Justice Department lawyer Matthew Donnelly. “How can we do that?”
The case is part of a larger effort under the right-wing Trump administration to crack down on alleged noncitizen voting ahead of the crucial November 3 midterm elections.
On October 15, less than three weeks before the midterm races, the Justice Department issued a complaint targeting California, a left-wing stronghold.

A Congolese health worker receives a vaccination in North Kivu province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, on October 16, 2026 [Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters]By Al Jazeera Staff, AP and ReutersPublished On 26 Oct 202626 Oct 2026
A nurse has been killed and another health worker severely injured after they were attacked while responding to an Ebola alert in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), according to the World Health Organization.
It was the latest in a series of attacks on health workers and responders that authorities say is hampering efforts to slow the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in the world.

The attack took place on Saturday in the town of Bafwasende in the DRC’s eastern Tshopo province, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said in a post on X on Sunday.
“Everyone working to protect communities from this deadly disease must be able to work in dignity and safety. Healthcare must always be protected,” he said.
The WHO’s regional director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi, also condemned the attack on X.
“Health is NOT a target,” he said. “Those responding to the Ebola outbreak must be protected. Misinformation and fear must never fuel violence.”
Local authorities have not yet commented on the attack or the suspects.

Port Huron, Michigan – United States President Donald Trump has sharpened his anti-Muslim attacks against Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, going so far as to suggest that Christmas would be cancelled if the progressive doctor won.
Trump visited Michigan on Sunday to shore up support for Republican candidates in the Midwestern state ahead of the midterm elections on November 3.

“He would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate,” Trump said of El-Sayed.
“I want him to have a metal detector.”
The president, whose popularity has been slipping in part due to the US-Israel war on Iran, spoke for nearly two hours to hundreds of supporters.
His remarks largely focused on Michigan’s Senate election, which is one of only about seven toss-up races for the upper chamber of Congress.
El-Sayed faces Republican candidate Mike Rogers for the state’s open Senate seat, and the race is considered crucial for Republicans to retain control of the 100-member Senate.

Lula delivers a victory speech after winning a fourth term in the presidential run-off in Brazil on October 25, 2026 [Andre Penner/AP Photo]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 26 Oct 202626 Oct 2026
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has secured a fourth nonconsecutive term after defeating right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in a run-off.
Bolsonaro, however, has called for Sunday’s vote to be annulled over an “unacceptable” two-hour voting extension granted by Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin despite both candidates having requested additional voting time.Flavio Bolsonaro speaks after the results of the presidential run-off in Brazil were announced on October 25, 2026 [Ton Molina/Getty Images]
The election results have drawn reactions across the world with leftist global figures celebrating Lula’s victory.
Here’s how the world reacted:
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum
Sheinbaum congratulated Lula in a post on X. “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won,” she wrote.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney
In his congratulatory post, Carney credited Lula with advancing relations between Canada and Brazil.
“Let us seize this opportunity to strengthen them further, together – to create new promising commercial prospects, protect the environment, and ensure greater prosperity for both our populations,” he wrote on X.
US officials and politicians
US President Donald Trump’s son Donald Trump Jr criticised the result, citing the two-hour voting time extension.
“If a conservative government in Brazil did this, everyone in the mainstream press in America would lose their minds, but I guess they’re just choosing to be silent because it’s all for the cause,” he said.
